blocks.p: Rei came back from Sumida in the killing afternoon heat, and the ledger had grown while the flat stood empty. It had never done that before. Every earlier addition had appeared in the small hours, in sleep's blind window. This one had come in daylight, while he was across the city with his hand on Iwata's thread. The timing was not lost on him.
The sulfur lay across the threshold exactly as he had left it, pale and dry. It told him nothing. It had been told to tell him nothing.
The thirty-fifth entry was short. It was in the leaning hand, the not-quite-Gin pressure. It did not record a favour granted. It recorded one offered and refused, and the refusal it named was Rei's.
R. would not set the weight down, it read, so the weight stays. We will try again when he is tired enough. He is nearly tired enough.... G.

So the count had always been a countdown. Rei saw it whole now, the way he had seen the timeline stand up and the spiral aim at Kita. The ledger had never been a list of the saved with Rei outside it taking notes. It was a list of the saved with a blank line kept open at the bottom. The blank line had had his name on it from the first night he came to the door. Everything since had been the Healer narrowing the distance between Rei and the moment he was tired enough to be helped. The spiral. The daylight favours. The note in his brother's hand. Iwata's tea, poured before he arrived. It was not racing him to Gin. It was waiting for him to arrive at it, exhausted and grateful. That was the only door it had ever needed anyone to walk through.

He should have felt hunted. Instead, for one clarifying second, he felt almost calm. A countdown, unlike a hunt, has a logic, and this logic was simple and terrible. It won when he stopped. It won when he broke. The only state it had no entry for was a man who kept moving while tired and refused to be grateful. That was the whole of his road now. Not to outrun the ledger. He could not. It wrote faster than he could read. His road was to stay, every hour, the one name it could not finish. Awake. Ungrateful. Still counting. Still his own.

He took out the folded note from that morning and laid the two side by side, the offer and the refusal recorded in the same patient hand. He was reading a conversation the Healer had been having with him for a week. Only one of them had been allowed to speak.

It was Tuesday. Rei remembered that with a small shock as the light went orange on the balcony. Gin's price list said that the ramen Gin always went to on Tuesdays was eight hundred and fifty yen for the tonkotsu. Worth it.

blocks.cap: The ramen counter where Gin ate on Tuesdays

blocks.p: Rei knew the place. He had been there with his brother a dozen times without ever understanding it was a habit. A narrow counter, eight stools, steam on the window. He sat on the stool Gin always took, ordered the tonkotsu, and ate all of it. The broth was thick and too salty and very good. The man behind the counter looked at him for a moment as if trying to remember where he had seen that jaw before, and then went back to his pots. Nobody asked Rei anything. It was the first full meal he had eaten in three days.
On the way home he stopped at the 7-Eleven on Kita-jūjō Nishi. Gin had written about it in a margin, on page thirty-four of the archive, in the section on what practitioners carry.

doc.title: Gin's archive. Margin of page 34
lines: The 7-Eleven on Kita-jūjō Nishi has a staff member who always works Thursday nights who asks how I am doing and appears to actually want to know. I go there after difficult cases.
I do not think she knows what I do. I think she can tell when someone needs to be asked a normal question by a normal person.
I have never documented her name because I do not want to look at her the way I look at cases.

blocks.p: It was not Thursday. The young man at the register had dyed hair and did not look up from restocking the cigarette shelf. Rei bought a can of hot coffee he did not need and sat on the stool by the window for twenty minutes, under the bright lights, doing nothing unusual. A tired office worker debated between two onigiri behind him. A delivery van idled at the kerb. Gin's page said this worked, and it did, a little.

doc.title: The Kombini Protocol. Ordinary Spaces as Stability Infrastructure
lines: Convenience stores at 3am are one of the most reliable stability recovery tools available. Bright lights. Ordinary transactions. Other ordinary people doing ordinary things. The kombini, where nothing significant ever happens, by design, is structurally cleaner than most spaces a practitioner encounters.
Eating a warm kombini meal. +3% stability. Standing at the counter, eating something hot, under fluorescent lights, while someone behind you debates which onigiri to buy.
Sitting in a kombini for 20 minutes doing nothing unusual. +2% stability. You do not have to try. You have to be there.
Your regular order at your regular place. +5% stability. The familiarity is the mechanic.

Near thin spots, active shrines, or suffering being ground, ordinary recovery is halved. You cannot kombini your way back from a deep clearance in Oji at 2am without first putting distance between yourself and the location.

blocks.p: Rei finished the coffee and thought about the woman on Thursday nights who asked Gin how he was. She would be here in two days. She would not know what to ask about. He hoped, absurdly, that she had noticed Gin had stopped coming.

Night came the way Obon nights come, lantern-lit and full of the returning dead. Back in the flat Rei did the things Gin's pages told him to do, in order, because order was something he could hold. He poured a salt line across the inside of the threshold, one continuous stream from the tub, no gaps. He sprinkled iron filings along it, so that anything that forced the line would pay for it. He put Gin's heavy cast-iron pan on the stove, because a steel knife does nothing and a cast-iron skillet works, and because Gin had cooked in it every Sunday of Rei's life.

Then he lit the gas ring under the kettle with his lighter, and sat down with the lighter still in his hand. He turned it over and over. It was a cheap thing, scratched silver, and he had carried it so long he no longer noticed he was holding it. He opened the archive at the section on inventory, and the lighter stopped in his fingers.

doc.title: Inventory and the Field Kit. Grounding Objects
lines: Every practitioner has one. An object that connects them to ordinary life when the veil layer is too loud, when they are close to the possession window and need something real to hold onto. The object is not magical. It is specific. The specificity is what makes it work.

Held during a stability crisis, +5% immediate recovery. Nearby during rest, +5% to total rest recovery. If you lose it, your stability ceiling drops 5% until it is recovered or replaced. Replacement takes one month. You cannot rush this.

The people I work with. Nakamura Aoi, ceramic bead bracelet. Kato Ryusei, a white chess piece. Katagiri Noa, small imperfect pottery bowl. Tsukishiro Haruki, dried flower, jacket pocket. Shimizu Ren, worn athletic glove, left hand only. Gin, unknown. The archive has a gap here.

doc.title: End of Inventory Notes. Personal Note. A Sunday. Quiet.
lines: Everyone has one. The ones who say they do not have one have one and do not know it yet. The object is not chosen. It accumulates.
Mine is not documented in this chapter. I wrote the entry twice and deleted it both times. Some things the archive holds back not because they are secret but because writing them down changes them.
Rei's is the lighter. He does not know that is what it is yet. He will.
G.U. Keys on the hook.

blocks.cap: Gin's keys, the object he signed at the end of every page

blocks.p: Rei sat with the lighter in his palm for a long time. Then he looked at the empty hook by the door, where Gin's keys had hung every day since Rei was small enough to be lifted up to reach them. Keys on the hook. Gin had ended almost every page of the archive with those three words. He had written that his own object was a gap, and then signed the gap at the bottom of every page for six years.
And on the night Gin went quiet, the hook had been empty, and the key had been lying on the walkway outside the door.

Rei did not let himself finish that thought. He closed his hand around the lighter instead and felt, faintly, something in him settle half an inch, the way a boat settles when someone steps into it who knows how.

He could not sleep yet, so he read. He read the chapter he had been avoiding, the one on reincarnation, because he remembered the night Gin had been writing it. Gin had been sitting at this table with a stack of very old files, and Rei had looked over his shoulder and asked what they were.

doc.title: Gin's preface, Chapter 12
lines: Rei came in last night while I was reviewing the Uedera family case files again, the fourth time I have gone through them this month.
He looked at what I was reading and said, those are really old. I said yes. He said, are they ours? I said, yes. He said, hm. And went to make tea and brought me a cup without asking.
He is sometimes very perceptive in ways that have nothing to do with the veil.
G.U.

blocks.p: Rei remembered the tea. He did not remember that he had said hm. He read on.

doc.title: CVD Entity Classification Reference. Chapter 12. Reincarnation. Research Classification. Contested
lines: Reincarnation is the only path that produces no detectable entity. The soul crosses, the self does not corrupt or dissolve, and it simply continues... inside a new life.
The CVD has seventeen documented cases of verifiable reincarnation over forty years. Its official position is unconfirmed hypothesis. That position has been unchanged for thirty-one years.

Karmic reincarnation. The soul enters a soulless neonate in a compatible family lineage. It does not arrive with memories but with orientations. Preferences, fears, relational patterns, ability profiles that do not match the family's genetic history.
Involuntary absorption. A dying person's extreme will to live creates a membrane vacuum that draws in a crossing soul. Neither party chose this. One body, two consciousnesses.
Children between about two and five sometimes describe places they have never been and people they never met. The memory window closes around age seven.

Multi-spectrum families show a progressive pattern across generations, each generation developing more paths than the previous, as if the soul carrying the capability is refining it over successive lifetimes.

doc.title: Margin, G.U.
lines: The Uedera family files. Each generation stronger than the previous. Each generation developing more paths.

I am not concluding that the soul currently living as me has lived in this family before. I am noting that the evidence is consistent with that conclusion and that I find myself thinking about it more than is probably strictly necessary.
The family files are on the desk. The tea is cold.

blocks.p: Each generation developing more paths. Rei thought of his own two registers, the low one and the searching one, which no file had ever measured properly because he had never let anything measure them. Gin had been sitting here working out whether the Uedera line kept coming back as itself. And then he had drunk the tea his little brother brought him and said nothing about it.

Rei put the archive down and sat with the two notes and the long torn strip of dates. He took his own pulse the way he would take a stranger's. Honestly. Clinically. Looking for the thing the Healer was waiting for.

He was tired. There was no use pretending the tiredness away. It lived behind his eyes and in the two flat registers he had not let himself feel in days. The thing wearing his brother had read it correctly, the way it read everyone. That was the whole of its terrible competence. He is nearly tired enough. Nearly. The word was doing more work than Rei wanted it to. Nearly was a confession. It meant the door was not open yet. It meant there was still a margin. It meant that tonight, this hour, he was still the unfinished entry and not the closed one.

He did the only thing the countdown had no answer for, which was the smallest thing. He decided to be tired and stay. Not heroically. He was too exhausted for heroism, and the Healer would only file heroism as another threshold it could help him across. He simply refused the rest, the way Iwata could not and the widow had never been given the chance to. He kept the page open. He wrote nothing in it. He let the long night be long.

There was a difference, he understood now, between the rest the Healer offered and the rest Gin had written down. The Healer's rest was a knot. Gin's rest was a bowl of ramen on a Tuesday, a can of coffee under bright lights, a lighter turned over and over in a hand that did not know it was holding on. One of them asked for gratitude. The other only asked him to come back to his own life.

Somewhere north of Kita his brother's body was sleeping a sleep that something else was dreaming. Somewhere closer, the ledger waited for the morning when Rei would be tired enough to be grateful. Between those two facts he sat awake and ungrateful and alive. It was, he understood, the only act of love the Healer had left him that it could not turn into a leash.

Before he slept, and he would sleep, he had to, the body keeps its own ledger and it was calling in its debts, he turned the strip of dates over. He started a new line at the bottom, on the blank the Healer had kept open. He did not write his gratitude there. He wrote the date, and beside it three words in his own unleaning hand, his own claim staked on the only page the thing had been allowed to fill.
still counting.... R.

Then he lay down in the heat, with both notes within reach and the lighter in his fist and the salt line white across the door. He let himself be tired, deliberately, openly, an entry that refused to close. Outside, the lanterns burned for the dead and the city forgot itself toward dawn. And the ledger, for the first time all week, had an answer in it that the Healer had not written.
